'''''Rhus typhina''''', the '''staghorn sumac''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RHTY|taxon=Rhus typhina|access-date=21 October 2015}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Anacardiaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to eastern North America. It is primarily found in southeastern Canada, the northeastern and midwestern United States, and the Appalachian Mountains,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://esp.cr.usgs.gov/data/atlas/little/rhustyph.pdf |publisher=United States Geological Survey |title=''Rhus typhina'' Range Map |access-date=2008-03-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120626032329/http://esp.cr.usgs.gov/data/atlas/little/rhustyph.pdf |archive-date=2012-06-26}}</ref> but it is widely cultivated as an ornamental throughout the [[temperate]] world. It is an [[invasive species]] in some parts of the world.

==Etymology==
The Latin [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''typhina'' is explained in [[Carl Linnaeus]] and Ericus Torner's description of the plant with the phrase "Ramis hirtis uti typhi cervini", meaning "the branches are hairy like [[antlers]] in velvet".

==Description==
[[File:Staghorn Sumac in McGregor.jpg|thumb|''Rhus typhina'' foliage in autumn]]
''Rhus typhina'' is a [[Plant sexuality#Individual plant sexuality|dioecious]], [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing up to {{cvt|5|m|ft|0}} tall by {{cvt|6|m|ft|0}} broad. It has alternate, pinnately compound leaves {{cvt|25|-|55|cm|0}} long, each with 9–31 serrate leaflets {{cvt|6–11|cm|in|frac=4}} long.<ref name=Uva>{{cite book |first1=Richard H. |last1=Uva |first2=Joseph C. |last2=Neal |first3=Joseph M. |last3=Ditomaso |title=Weeds of The Northeast |location=Ithaca, NY |publisher=Cornell University Press |year=1997 |pages=326–327 |isbn=0-8014-3391-6 }}</ref> Leaf petioles and stems are densely covered in rust-colored hairs. The velvety texture and the forking pattern of the branches, reminiscent of [[antler]]s, have led to the common name "stag's horn sumac".<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|pages=1136}}</ref> Staghorn sumac grows as female or male clones.<ref>{{FEIS |genus=Rhus |species=typhina |type=tree |last=Sullivan |first=Janet |date=1994}}</ref>

Small, greenish-white through yellowish flowers occur in dense terminal panicles, and small, green through reddish [[drupes]] occur in dense infructescences.<ref name=Uva/> Flowers occur from May through July and fruit ripens from June through September in this species' native range.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nsl.fs.fed.us/wpsm/Rhus.pdf |publisher=USDA Forest Service |website=Woody Plant Seed Manual |title=''Rhus'' |access-date=2009-07-14 |archive-date=2009-02-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090219083830/http://nsl.fs.fed.us/wpsm/Rhus.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Infructescences are {{cvt|10|-|20|cm|in|0}} long and {{cvt|4|-|6|cm|in|frac=4}} broad at their bases. Fall foliage is brilliant shades of red, orange and yellow.<ref name=RHSAZ /> Fruit can remain on plants from late summer through spring. It is eaten by many birds in winter.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=327}}</ref>

Staghorn sumac spreads by seeds and [[rhizomes]] and forms clones often with the older shoots in the center and younger shoots around central older ones.<ref name=Uva/> Large clones can grow from [[wikt:ortet|ortets]] in several years.

In late summer some shoots have galls on leaf undersides, caused by the sumac leaf gall aphid, ''[[Melaphis rhois]]''. The galls are not markedly harmful to the tree.

==Cultivation==
Staghorn sumac is an ornamental plant which provides interest throughout the year; though its vigorous suckering habit makes it unsuitable for smaller gardens. It can grow under a wide array of conditions, but is most often found in dry and poor soil on which other plants cannot survive.<ref name=Uva/> Some landscapers remove all but the top branches to create a "crown" effect in order to resemble a small palm tree. Numerous [[cultivars]] have been developed for garden use, of which the following have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:<ref>{{cite web

==Uses==
[[File:20150420Rhus typhina1.jpg|thumb|''Rhus typhina'' fruit]]

The fruits of sumacs are edible.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=250|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> They can be soaked and washed in cold water, strained, sweetened and made into a [[lemonade]]-like drink called [[sumac-ade]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Lee Allen |last=Peterson |title=Edible Wild Plants |location=New York |publisher=Houghton Mifflin |year=1977 |isbn=0-395-20445-3 |page=186 }}</ref> The drink extract can also be used to make jelly. The shoots can be peeled and eaten raw.<ref>Thayer, S. (2006). The Forager's Harvest. Forager's Harvest.</ref><ref name=":0" /> The fruit was found to have certain natural antioxidant and antimicrobial properties.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kossah |first1=Rima |last2=Zhang |first2=Hao |last3=Chen |first3=Wei |date=2011-01-01 |title=Antimicrobial and antioxidant activities of Chinese sumac (Rhus typhina L.) fruit extract |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0956713510001684 |journal=Food Control |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=128–132 |doi=10.1016/j.foodcont.2010.06.002 |issn=0956-7135|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

All parts of the staghorn sumac, except the roots, can be used as both a [[natural dye]] and as a [[mordant]]. The plant is rich in [[tannins]] and can be added to other dye baths to improve light [[Colour fastness|fastness]]. The leaves may be harvested in the summer and the bark all year round.<ref>{{cite book |first=Jenny |last=Dean |title=Wild Color: The Complete Guide to Making and Using Natural Dyes |url=https://archive.org/details/wildcolor00dean |url-access=registration |location=New York |publisher=Watson-Guptill |year=1999 |page=[https://archive.org/details/wildcolor00dean/page/123 123] |isbn=978-0-8230-5727-6 }}</ref>

The timber provides high [[chatoyance]], with an average value above 20 PZC.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sumac |url=https://www.chatometry.com/sumac/ |access-date=2025-07-27 |website=PZC Chatometry |language=it-IT}}</ref>
